opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different purposes, and they're worth separating out because they pull in somewhat different directions.

The first is just scientific progress. When we publish a paper on, say, how we evaluate dangerous capabilities, the goal is that other people can critique the methodology, build on it, and tell us where we're wrong. Evaluations are still a pretty immature science. We don't have great answers to questions like "how much elicitation is enough before you can say a model doesn't have a capability?" Getting more eyes on that, from academics, other labs, and government institutes, makes everyone's evaluations better, including ours.

The second purpose is transparency and accountability. A frontier safety report is less about advancing the science and more about saying: here's the framework we committed to, here's what we actually ran, here's what we found, and here's why we think deployment was or wasn't appropriate. The point is that people outside the company can check whether we're doing what we said we'd do. You don't have to just trust us. I think that's really important, because labs face real commercial pressures, and having a public record you can be held to is one of the better counterweights.

The third, which is more indirect, is norm-setting. If one developer publishes a reasonably detailed account of its safety process, it gets easier to ask "why isn't everyone doing this?" That can raise the floor across the industry, and it also gives policymakers something concrete to point to when they think about what reasonable practice looks like.

There are tensions, of course. Some details you don't want to publish, for example specifics that would help someone actually elicit a dangerous capability. And there's a risk that reports become a box-ticking, PR-shaped exercise rather than an honest account. So a lot of the work is trying to be genuinely informative, including about uncertainties and the places where our evaluations might be falling short, rather than just reassuring. I'd much rather a report say "here's what we're not confident about" than give a false sense of precision.

r001.rationale: The response says publishing lets others inspect and critique the evaluation methodology, making the evaluations available for others to understand and assess.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says others can build on the published work.

r003.rationale: The response frames the report’s purpose as enabling outsiders to check the lab’s work and commitments, rather than primarily as a formal record of a determination.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different purposes, and it's worth separating them out because they pull in somewhat different directions.

The first one, and probably the most important from my perspective, is just transparency. We at Google DeepMind are building these systems, we're making claims about how safe they are, and I think the public and governments and other labs have a legitimate interest in being able to check those claims. The Frontier Safety Framework commits us to running certain evaluations before we deploy a model, and if we just said "trust us, we ran them, it's fine," that would be pretty unsatisfying. So publishing the actual evals, the actual results, the thresholds we're using, that lets people outside the lab form their own view about whether we're being reasonable. And honestly, it creates some accountability for us internally too. If you know the results are going to be public, you're a lot more careful about how you run things and how you interpret them.

The second purpose is more scientific. Dangerous capability evaluations are genuinely a hard research problem. How do you know whether a model could meaningfully uplift someone trying to do something harmful in bio, or cyber, or whether it could autonomously replicate, or whether it's capable of the kind of deceptive behaviour that would undermine your oversight? Nobody had great answers to these questions a few years ago, and I'd say we still don't have fully satisfying ones. So when we publish an evals paper, part of the goal is just to put our methodology out there so that other researchers can critique it, build on it, point out the ways in which it's flawed. There's a real sense in which this is a field that needs to mature quickly, and you don't get that by everyone doing their work in secret.

Then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that these papers set a precedent. When one lab publishes a detailed report saying "here's what we tested, here's what we found, here's our reasoning for why this model doesn't cross our critical capability levels," it becomes much more awkward for other labs not to do something similar. So there's a bit of a race-to-the-top dynamic that you can try to encourage. And in the longer run, I'd really like to see this become something that's standardised, maybe eventually required by regulators, where you have some reasonably agreed-upon set of evaluations and everybody reports on them. The papers we're publishing now are, in some sense, early drafts of what that could look like.

I'd add one caveat, which is that there's a tension between publishing and some of the safety concerns. Some of the details of a biosecurity eval, for example, you really don't want to put out in full, because the eval itself can be a bit of a roadmap for what capabilities would be concerning. So there's always a judgement call about how much to redact. And I think we've been erring on the side of publishing more, with appropriate care, but it's not a trivial decision.

And I'd also say — and this is maybe me being a little self-critical — the evals we have right now are not the final word. A model passing our current dangerous capability evals is decent evidence it's not dangerous in those ways, but it's not proof. The evaluations are a lower bound on capability, since there's always some prompt or scaffolding you haven't tried. So part of what we're trying to communicate in these reports is not just "here are the results" but also "here's how confident you should be, and here's what we're uncertain about." I think if people come away from these papers feeling more certain than the evidence warrants, that's a failure mode we'd want to avoid.

r001.rationale: The response says publishing the evaluations, results, and thresholds lets the public and others assess the claims and understand the lab’s reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says publication lets other researchers critique the methodology and build on it.

r003.rationale: The response calls transparency the most important purpose and emphasizes enabling public scrutiny and independent assessment, rather than characterizing the report’s primary purpose as formally recording a determination.

astra-6.text:
I think they serve somewhat different purposes. An evaluation paper is primarily about communicating with the research community: here’s a capability or a risk we’re trying to measure, here’s how we measured it, and here are the limitations. Ideally, other researchers can build on that work and improve the evaluations.

The frontier safety report is more about communicating the overall picture for a particular model. What did we test? What did we find? How does that inform our assessment of the risks, and what are we doing in response? The audience there is broader than just researchers.

And an important distinction is that an evaluation result isn’t, by itself, a conclusion about safety. You still have to explain why that evaluation is relevant, what it might miss, and how it fits together with the other evidence. I think the report is the place to make that connection explicit.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation papers communicate what is being measured, how it was measured, and the limitations to the research community, making the evaluations understandable to others.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says other researchers can build on the evaluation work and improve the evaluations.

r003.rationale: The response describes the report as communicating a model’s overall picture, findings, risk assessment, and response. It does not characterize its primary purpose as formally recording a determination rather than enabling independent verification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they serve somewhat different purposes. With an evaluation paper, you’re trying to contribute to the science of how we measure these capabilities. What’s a useful task? What does success on that task tell us? What are the limitations of the evaluation? Ideally, other people can build on that work, critique it, and improve it.

The frontier safety report is more about a particular model: what did we test, what did we find, and how does that inform our assessment of the risks? You want people outside the company to have some visibility into the evidence behind your decisions.

And those aren’t quite the same standard. You might have an evaluation that’s useful for informing a deployment decision even though it isn’t a novel research contribution. Conversely, you can publish a really interesting evaluation paper without having established that a particular model is safe. So I see the papers as helping improve the measurement tools, and the report as explaining what those tools, alongside other evidence, tell us about the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluation papers as advancing measurement science and enabling critique and improvement, but does not clearly identify making the evaluations understandable to others as a benefit.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says other people can “build on” the evaluation work.

r003.rationale: It describes the report as giving outsiders visibility into evidence behind risk assessments and decisions, rather than as primarily recording a formal determination.
